text: Over the past decade, a long list of organizations has had sensitive data exposed through a publicly readable S3 bucket or Azure Blob container — telecoms, consulting firms, media companies, government contractors, usually holding customer records or internal documents. In every case, the cloud provider's infrastructure was never breached. The bucket was simply reachable by anyone who found its name.

The root causes are a short, repeatable list. A legacy ACL grants access to the special AllUsers or Everyone group — easy to set by accident when copying permissions, and easy to miss since ACLs don't show up where most engineers look first. A bucket policy or container access level gets set public for convenience, often temporarily for a static site or shared download, then never gets reverted. And nobody watches for drift — a setting private on day one can be flipped later by anyone with sufficient permissions, unnoticed until someone outside the organization finds it.

S3 Block Public Access is deliberately blunt: four settings that override any ACL or bucket policy that would otherwise grant public access. At the account level, it applies to every bucket, including future ones, which is why security teams enable it account-wide as a baseline. At the bucket level, it's an exception for the rare bucket that genuinely needs to be public. Turned on together at the account level, no individual bucket owner can accidentally make a bucket public again, regardless of what gets configured on it afterward.

Azure Storage has a parallel structure. "Allow Blob public access" is an account-level setting that, disabled, makes it impossible for any container in that account to be public no matter its own setting — the direct analog of Block Public Access. Container public access level is set per container: Private, Blob for anonymous read of blob data only, or Container, the most dangerous, allowing anonymous read plus full listing. That per-container setting only matters at all if the account-level setting permits it, and Azure Policy can enforce the disabled state across a whole subscription.

Two more controls round this out. Private endpoints and VPC endpoints route traffic to the storage service entirely off the public internet, and a policy can require traffic arrive only that way. And continuous drift detection — AWS Config rules, Azure Policy — evaluates configuration on an ongoing basis rather than just at deployment, catching a setting that silently drifted back toward public. Encryption never substitutes for any of this: a public ACL on an encrypted object still produces a publicly readable object, because encryption protects against channels outside the normal read path, not the read path itself.

Next lesson steps back from any single control to the question that should come before all of them — data classification — and why writing a meaningful DLP rule depends on having classified the data it's meant to protect.
